claim: Invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is the leading cause of death from gynecologic cancer among women in developed countries.
source: Invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is the leading cause of death from gynecologic cancer among women in developed countries (Siegel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2016

claim: Most women with EOC present with advanced stage disease, where 5 year survival rates average 25–30%.
source: Most women with EOC present with advanced stage disease, where 5 year survival rates average 25–30%, highlighting the need for an effective screening strategy.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about EOC prognosis

claim: Two large-scale randomized clinical trials involving ultrasound and CA125 (PLCO and UKCTOCS) did not demonstrate a meaningful impact on overall survival from EOC.
source: Unfortunately, two large-scale randomized clinical trials involving ultrasound and CA125, including the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer (PLCO) trial and the United Kingdom Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS) trial did not demonstrate a meaningful impact on overall survival from EOC (Zhu et al., 2011; Jacobs et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2011 and Jacobs et al., 2016

claim: CA125 can detect advanced disease but has poorer sensitivity for early stage and non-serous cancers.
source: These and other non-experimental longitudinal studies reaffirm CA125 can detect advanced disease but with poorer sensitivity for early stage and non-serous cancers.
evidence: Supported by reference to longitudinal studies

claim: CA125 has limited specificity, with the majority of abnormal CA125 values being the result of non-gynecologic malignancies or benign gynecologic conditions.
source: In addition, CA125 has limited specificity, with the majority of abnormal CA125 values being the result of non-gynecologic malignancies or benign gynecologic conditions (Moss et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss et al., 2005

claim: Adding more biomarkers to CA125 did not improve screening in a re-analysis of the PLCO data and a recent longitudinal study from EPIC.
source: The hope that adding more biomarkers to CA125 would improve screening was not realized in a re-analysis of the PLCO data as well as a recent longitudinal study from the European Prospective Investigation of Nutrition and Cancer (Zhu et al., 2011; Terry et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2011 and Terry et al., 2016

claim: Several panels including CA125 have received FDA approval for differential diagnosis of EOC to encourage referral to centers with greater expertise.
source: In a separate strategy to improve EOC outcome, several panels (which have CA125 as part of them) have received FDA approval to be used in the differential diagnosis of EOC to encourage referral of EOC cases to centers with greater expertise in cancer surgery and chemotherapeutic treatment (Karst and Drapkin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karst and Drapkin, 2010

claim: FDA-approved panels including CA125 have not been effective for early diagnosis of EOC.
source: However, these have not been effective for early diagnosis.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion about FDA-approved panels

claim: Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have shown great potential for diagnosis or early detection of EOC.
source: Among the alternatives to serum proteins for the diagnosis or early detection of EOC, circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have shown great potential (Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2016

claim: miRNAs are short (18–24 nucleotide) non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression through post-transcriptional modification of mRNA transcripts.
source: miRNAs are short (18–24 nucleotide) non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression through post-transcriptional modification of mRNA transcripts.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about miRNA biology

claim: PCR amplifies detection of rare transcripts in blood.
source: miRNAs have several advantages over protein measures: (1) PCR amplifies detection of rare transcripts in blood
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about PCR technology

claim: All miRNAs use the same units of measure, easing incorporation into multiplexed panels.
source: (2) all miRNAs use the same units of measure, easing incorporation into multiplexed panels
evidence: Stated as a property of miRNA measurement

claim: miRNAs play a critical role in ovarian cancer biology.
source: (3) miRNAs play a critical role in ovarian cancer biology, whereas the function of CA125 is unknown (Deb et al., 2017; Katz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deb et al., 2017 and Katz et al., 2015

claim: The function of CA125 is unknown.
source: (3) miRNAs play a critical role in ovarian cancer biology, whereas the function of CA125 is unknown (Deb et al., 2017; Katz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deb et al., 2017 and Katz et al., 2015

claim: Non-invasive sampling of circulating miRNAs has a clear advantage over analytes obtained through biopsy.
source: Moreover, non-invasive sampling of circulating miRNAs has a clear advantage over analytes obtained through biopsy (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016

claim: Preliminary studies have suggested that circulating miRNAs profiles are altered in women with ovarian cancer.
source: Preliminary studies have suggested that circulating miRNAs profiles are altered in women with ovarian cancer (Nakamura et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2013; Langhe et al., 2015; Resnick et al., 2009; Zuberi et al., 2015; Samuel and Carter, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: miRNAs have prognostic significance for EOC survival.
source: In addition, miRNAs have prognostic significance for EOC survival (Merritt et al., 2008; Bagnoli et al., 2016; Cramer and Elias, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Merritt et al., 2008, Bagnoli et al., 2016, and Cramer and Elias, 2016

claim: Efforts to develop a diagnostic signature based on circulating miRNAs have been hampered by issues regarding statistical approach, reproducibility across technology platforms, and biologic heterogeneity of EOC.
source: However, efforts to develop a diagnostic signature based on circulating miRNAs have been hampered by issues regarding the best statistical approach to develop a model, reproducibility of miRNA measurement across technology platforms (e.g. qPCR, next generation sequencing, microarray), and the biologic heterogeneity of EOC (Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2016

claim: The study population comprised 179 women selected from three independent prospective studies (ERASMOS, PMP, and NECC).
source: To produce our diagnostic circulating miRNA signature from human sera, we constructed a study population of pre-treatment (prior to either surgery or chemotherapy) subjects comprising 179 women selected from three independent prospective studies (ERASMOS, PMP, and NECC) (Table 1).
evidence: Describes the study design and sample collection

claim: ERASMOS contributed consecutive cases presenting for evaluation of an adnexal mass.
source: ERASMOS contributed consecutive cases presenting for evaluation of an adnexal mass, while PMP allowed enrichment of the population for specific histopathologic diagnoses.
evidence: Describes the study design

claim: PMP allowed enrichment of the population for specific histopathologic diagnoses.
source: ERASMOS contributed consecutive cases presenting for evaluation of an adnexal mass, while PMP allowed enrichment of the population for specific histopathologic diagnoses.
evidence: Describes the study design

claim: NECC added healthy controls age-matched to PMP.
source: NECC added healthy controls age-matched to PMP.
evidence: Describes the study design

claim: After randomization, the training and testing sets were demographically similar.
source: After the randomization, the training and testing sets were demographically similar, and there were no differences in the distribution of histopathological diagnoses between the sets (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 2

claim: There were no differences in the distribution of histopathological diagnoses between the training and testing sets.
source: After the randomization, the training and testing sets were demographically similar, and there were no differences in the distribution of histopathological diagnoses between the sets (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 2

claim: The neural network model employing miRNA expression fold changes had an AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81–0.99).
source: Although many of the models performed well, the neural network model employing miRNA expression fold changes was the only model to meet our pre-specified statistical objective with an AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81–0.99; p=0.03 over a theoretical AUC of 0.75).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the testing set

claim: The neural network model was the only model to meet the pre-specified statistical objective (p=0.03 over a theoretical AUC of 0.75).
source: Although many of the models performed well, the neural network model employing miRNA expression fold changes was the only model to meet our pre-specified statistical objective with an AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81–0.99; p=0.03 over a theoretical AUC of 0.75).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The neural network consisted of 14 individual miRNAs with seven neurons in the hidden layer.
source: The network consisted of 14 individual miRNAs with seven neurons in the hidden layer (Source code 1).
evidence: Describes the structure of the neural network model

claim: The neural network worked equally well on adjusted and unadjusted raw datasets with an AUC of 0.93 (95%CI: 0.89–0.98) on the training and 0.90 (95%CI 0.80–0.99) on the testing set.
source: The neural network worked equally well on the adjusted and unadjusted raw datasets with an AUC of 0.93 (95%CI: 0.89–0.98) on the training and 0.90 (95%CI 0.80–0.99) on the testing set (Figure 3; Supplementary file 1A [by model] and 1B [by sample]).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary files

claim: The neural network worked equally well for older and younger patients.
source: In post-hoc secondary analyses, the neural network worked equally well for older and younger patients, serous and non-serous histologies, and early and advanced stage disease (Supplementary file 2A-C).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc secondary analyses in supplementary files

claim: The neural network worked equally well for serous and non-serous histologies.
source: In post-hoc secondary analyses, the neural network worked equally well for older and younger patients, serous and non-serous histologies, and early and advanced stage disease (Supplementary file 2A-C).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc secondary analyses in supplementary files

claim: The neural network worked equally well for early and advanced stage disease.
source: In post-hoc secondary analyses, the neural network worked equally well for older and younger patients, serous and non-serous histologies, and early and advanced stage disease (Supplementary file 2A-C).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc secondary analyses in supplementary files

claim: Serum CA125 data were available for 120 subjects.
source: Serum CA125 data were available for 120 subjects (Supplementary file 1B and 3A).
evidence: Describes the available data

claim: Among 120 subjects with CA125 data, the neural network (AUC 0.93; 95% CI 0.88–0.97) significantly outperformed CA125 (AUC 0.74; 95% CI 0.65–0.83; p=0.001).
source: Among these, the neural network (AUC 0.93; 95% CI 0.88–0.97) significantly outperformed CA125 (AUC 0.74; 95% CI 0.65–0.83; p=0.001; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 4

claim: The primary advantage of the neural network over CA125 was avoiding false positives (8/43 for the neural network versus 23/43 for CA125; p=0.002).
source: The primary advantage of the neural network over CA125 was avoiding false positives (8/43 for the neural network versus 23/43 for CA125; p=0.002) (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison in supplementary file

claim: The neural network and CA125 levels were independent of one another.
source: Notably, the neural network and CA125 levels were independent of one another (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Using the neural network and CA125 in a tiered testing strategy would increase the probability of a false positive test result from 4.2% (5/120) to 19.2% (23/120).
source: We tested using the neural network and CA125 in a tiered testing strategy, subjecting all negative neural network algorithm results to a second review with CA125, but found this would increase the probability of a false positive test result from 4.2% (5/120) to 19.2% (23/120) and a false negative rate from 5.8% (7/120) to 13.3% (16/120) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Using the neural network and CA125 in a tiered testing strategy would increase the false negative rate from 5.8% (7/120) to 13.3% (16/120).
source: We tested using the neural network and CA125 in a tiered testing strategy, subjecting all negative neural network algorithm results to a second review with CA125, but found this would increase the probability of a false positive test result from 4.2% (5/120) to 19.2% (23/120) and a false negative rate from 5.8% (7/120) to 13.3% (16/120) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Initial screening with CA125 followed by neural network yielded only three additional correctly diagnosed cases of invasive cancer at the expense of 19 additional false positive results.
source: The alternative of initial screening with CA125 followed by neural network yielded only three additional correctly diagnosed cases of invasive cancer at the expense of 19 additional false positive results.
evidence: Supported by analysis of tiered testing strategy

claim: The neural network perfectly classified patients in the Keller et al. training set (AUC 1.00, 95% CI 1.00–1.00).
source: The neural network perfectly classified patients in the training set (AUC 1.00, 95% CI 1.00–1.00) and provided very good discriminatory power on the testing set (AUC 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.00), with an overall sensitivity of 75% and specificity of 100%.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the Keller et al. dataset

claim: The neural network provided very good discriminatory power on the Keller et al. testing set (AUC 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.00), with an overall sensitivity of 75% and specificity of 100%.
source: The neural network perfectly classified patients in the training set (AUC 1.00, 95% CI 1.00–1.00) and provided very good discriminatory power on the testing set (AUC 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.00), with an overall sensitivity of 75% and specificity of 100%.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the Keller et al. dataset

claim: The signature was specific to ovarian cancer compared to all other diagnoses in the Keller et al. dataset.
source: The signature was specific to ovarian cancer compared to all other diagnoses, as it did not show any clinically-efficient diagnostic capabilities for any of the 12 other morbidities analysed in the set and showed good performance in distinguishing ovarian cancer samples against all other diagnoses combined (AUC 0.92, 95% CI 0.82–1.00) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The neural network did not show clinically-efficient diagnostic capabilities for any of the 12 other morbidities analysed in the Keller et al. dataset.
source: The signature was specific to ovarian cancer compared to all other diagnoses, as it did not show any clinically-efficient diagnostic capabilities for any of the 12 other morbidities analysed in the set and showed good performance in distinguishing ovarian cancer samples against all other diagnoses combined (AUC 0.92, 95% CI 0.82–1.00) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The neural network showed good performance in distinguishing ovarian cancer samples against all other diagnoses combined (AUC 0.92, 95% CI 0.82–1.00) in the Keller et al. dataset.
source: The signature was specific to ovarian cancer compared to all other diagnoses, as it did not show any clinically-efficient diagnostic capabilities for any of the 12 other morbidities analysed in the set and showed good performance in distinguishing ovarian cancer samples against all other diagnoses combined (AUC 0.92, 95% CI 0.82–1.00) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: Global sensitivity analysis reduced the neural network to only seven miRNAs (miR-29a-3p, miR-92a-3p, miR-200c-3p, miR-320c, miR-335–5 p, miR-450b-5p, and miR-1307–5 p) plus four normalizers (miR-423–3 p, miR-191–5 p, miR-221–3 p, and miR-103a-3p).
source: We then performed a global sensitivity analysis on the best neural network for qPCR data and iteratively removed the variables which did the least in terms of improving the classifier's performance. This reduced the neural network to only seven miRNAs (miR-29a-3p, miR-92a-3p, miR-200c-3p, miR-320c, miR-335–5 p, miR-450b-5p, and miR-1307–5 p) plus four normalizers (miR-423–3 p, miR-191–5 p, miR-221–3 p, and miR-103a-3p).
evidence: Describes the optimization process for the qPCR model

claim: The qPCR-based neural network performed well with an AUC 0.89 on the training set and AUC 0.80 on the testing set.
source: The resulting network performed well with an AUC 0.89 on the training set and AUC 0.80 on the testing set.

claim: In the Polish external validation set, the neural network had a positive predictive value of 91.3% (95% CI: 73.3–97.6%).
source: In this population, the neural network had a positive predictive value of 91.3% (95% CI: 73.3–97.6%) and a negative predictive value of 78.6% (95% CI: 64.2–88.2%) with an AUC of 0.85 (Figure 6).

claim: In the Polish external validation set, the neural network had a negative predictive value of 78.6% (95% CI: 64.2–88.2%).

source: Circulating levels of all three miRNAs decreased within 72 hr of tumor removal, with significant changes for miR-200a-3p and miR-200c-3p (Figure 7A–D).

claim: There is limited overlap between miRNAs identified in recent studies and miRNAs that emerged from the current analysis.

evidence: Comparison to prior studies

claim: Limited sample numbers in prior studies diminish the statistical robustness of the results.
source: One possible cause of this difference is the limited number of samples examined in these studies. For example, in Langhe et al, a training set of 5 serous ovarian carcinomas and five benign serous cystadenomas were selected for the initial experiments. The validation set was 20 serous ovarian carcinomas and 20 benign serous cystadenomas. In Resnick et al, 28 ovarian carcinoma patients and 15 healthy controls were used to identify to differential expression of circulating miRNAs. Such limited numbers diminish the statistical robustness of the results.
evidence: Inference based on comparison to prior studies

claim: A study systematically compared 12 different miRNA expression platforms and found a 12-fold difference between the highest and lowest number of detected miRNA when identical samples were profiled by different platforms.
